title: Windows 11 is collecting data on which coding agents and developer tools you use
titleZh: Windows 11 is collecting data on which coding agents and developer tools you use
author: cwaffles
relevanceReason: 命中 5 个 AI/科技关键词。
summaryRaw: Reverse engineering Windows 11's MissionControlAggregator reveals coding-agent and developer-tool usage bits in a diagnostic ETW report.I recently asked AI to help me look through the latest Windows binaries for undocumented features and functionality. Among the leads it turned up, one list immediately caught my attention: coding agents such as codex.exe, claude.exe, copilot.exe, and cursor.exe, alongside familiar developer tools such as python.exe, dotnet.exe, gcc.exe, and code.exe.Why would a Windows system DLL need a list of coding agents and developer tools?The names were in MissionControlAggregator.dll. I asked the agent to follow the references and dig into what the DLL actually does. That led from a handful of string comparisons to a running Windows component that records which coding agents and developer tools have been used, saves that information locally, and reports it to Windows Diagnostics. And unless you have opted out of the “optional” diagnostic data (which is enabled by default), the data is uploaded to Microsoft.I shared the initial finding on X. This post includes more details about the investigation behind it.Following the namesOpening the DLL in Binary Ninja made the first lead easy to see. These were explicit executable names embedded in a Windows component:Following the references showed that the names were used in comparisons. There are four CLI-agent slots checking copilot.exe, claude.exe, codex.exe, and agy.exe, with extensionless equivalents on the WSL route. Five desktop-agent slots check github.exe, claude.exe, codex.exe, cursor.exe, and antigravity.exe.Here is one of the comparisons against codex.exe:The compiler-generated C++ names are unwieldy, so I will call these functions executable-name matchers. For reference, one related matcher is std::_Func_impl_no_alloc<<lambda_340dfe7e962ab225b6ac33bc664bd54f>, bool, std::basic_string_view<wchar_t, std::char_traits<wchar_t>> const&, Microsoft::Diagnostics::MissionControlAggregator::Utils::AppType>::_Do_call. The screenshot shows another lambda instantiation performing the same kind of name comparison.The feature guarding the new agent checks has a particularly direct name: CLICodingAgentUsage, feature ID 62580080.And the list extends beyond AI agents. The same component checks for node.exe, python.exe, dotnet.exe, gcc.exe, clang.exe, gdb.exe, javac.exe, devenv.exe, and code.exe, among others. Those checks feed broader developer-tool categories. Some of these checks also verify the publisher: the Node.js slot expects Node.js Foundation, Python expects Python Software Foundation, and the .NET and Visual Studio slots expect Microsoft Corporation. The compiler/debugger group containing GCC and Clang has no additional publisher check in this path.Where does the DLL get this information?The next question was whether the component scans running processes itself. Following Aggregator::OnLoad revealed that it subscribes to existing Windows events instead.For Windows programs, it consumes KernelProcess.AppStateChangeSummary and Win32kTraceLogging.AppInteractivitySummary. These provide application identities that its handlers parse and pass to the matchers. For WSL, it consumes Microsoft.Windows.Lxss.Manager.Exec and ExecCritical, using the imageName field. A regular Windows codex.exe can therefore reach the CLI-agent checks through the app-state summary route; this is not limited to Linux programs running inside WSL.The relevant flow looks like this:Aggregator::OnLoad ├─ WSL Exec / ExecCritical │ └─ ProcessWslExecEvent → CLI agent matchers ├─ KernelProcess.AppStateChangeSummary │ └─ ProcessAppStateChangeSummaryEvent → CLI agent matchers └─ Win32kTraceLogging.AppInteractivitySummary └─ ProcessAppInteractivitySummaryEvent → desktop agent matchers

Aggregator::OnUnload / intermediate timer └─ PersistentState::SaveToDisk A successful match sets a slot in the aggregator’s state. Later, ReportCohorts<12,4,5> turns those slots into bitsets and emits a report named Segments.SubCohorts. The numbers correspond to twelve broader tool categories, four CLI agents, and five desktop agents.ETW (Event Tracing for Windows) is the mechanism carrying that report. In this case, it is a self-describing TraceLogging event. Rather than writing the executable names into every report, the component assigns each category a bit. A set Codex bit means the matching tool was observed during the reporting window.The source events also include runtime, time in focus, interaction counters, and resource usage. This component appears to discard those details and record only a bitmap of which agents were observed. The report’s timestamps describe the collection window, not how long each agent was used.Although I found no prompt text or source code in this report, collecting which agents and developer tools someone uses already has significant privacy implications.Is it actually running on a normal machine?Strings and code are a useful lead, but I wanted to see the component running. I checked my Parallels Windows 11 ARM64 VM, build 26200.9974. Its MissionControlAggregator.dll was version 10.0.26100.9818, and CLICodingAgentUsage was already enabled as a service experiment. I had not manually enabled the feature.DiagTrack, the Connected User Experiences and Telemetry service, was also already running with its startup type set to Automatic. It starts a separate AggregatorHost.exe process, and that process loads the DLL. The following administrative PowerShell commands show the service, its child process, and the loaded module:PS> Get-Service DiagTrack | Format-Table Name,Status,StartType -AutoSize
Name Status StartType ---- ------ --------- DiagTrack Running Automatic

comments.author: dead_hn_theory
comments.textRawHtml:
For anyone on the fence about switching from Windows to Linux: it takes about a week, if that, of adjusting. If most of what you do is on the Web already (and the services you use provide a Web-based client), you have nothing to lose but your chains.

Take your pick - Ubuntu, Fedora, someone else mentioned Mint. All fine choices, no wrong answers.

children.author: cortesoft
children.textRawHtml:
As someone who owns and operaters Linux, Windows, and Mac systems at home, this just isn't true for a lot of people.

I have to keep my gaming PC as Windows because I can't play Madden, EA FC, or PUBG on my Linux machines nor my Steam Deck (unless I install windows). They all require kernel level anti-cheats that are only supported on Windows.

You also can't play a ton of other very popular games (that I don't happen to play, but millions do) like Call of Duty, Fortnite, League of Legends, Battlefield, etc. Those games have millions of players.

And this is just for gaming. There are plenty of other bits of software that don't run on Linux, even with all of the amazing work that has gone into compatibility tools like WINE.

I am not saying that many people shouldn't explore moving to Linux from Windows, but I don't think it is helpful to say everyone can switch without at least mentioning any of the reasons people can't.

children.author: autuni
children.textRawHtml:
You can still recommend that people switch, if people have their own specific reasons why they can't, they won't. It's not like anyone mandates that people switch.

For gaming, most games don't have issues. For the games that do, if enough people actually do switch, it gives more incentives for their publishers to make their games work on Linux without issues. We are also no longer starved for potential alternative games that are very similar and do work on Linux.

Most other software has very good alternatives by now.

So overall I do think it is reasonable to recommend people make the switch rather than stay a hostage of a system they don't like because some software providers refuse to offer an alternative on Linux. If you have specific reasons not to switch, don't switch.

children.author: rat9988
children.textRawHtml:
When you advice people to switch, you should be transparent about the limitations.

What is the point of the advice if it doesn't give you any useful information?

children.author: piaste
children.textRawHtml:
There's a wide, wide, wide gap between "doesn't give any useful information" and "explicitly list all software and hardware that doesn't support Linux, like a medicine informational sheet".

Saying 'you should switch to Linux because it respects your privacy and doesn't frustrate you with ads' is perfectly reasonable advice. The details come later and are based on what that person needs (why even mention gaming DRM if the user isn't a gamer, for example?).

children.author: no2_fresh
children.textRawHtml:
I feel this is the biggest problem with the Linux community.

-Linux is fully customizable!, they'll say.

Well, so it your house. You could move the kitchen and the bathroom, but it's not done over night, and you need the skills to do so.

That beeing said, I've made the switch about at year ago. I do miss some software, I havent gotten to play Battlefield 6 because of it, but i really don't miss Windows at all.

children.author: docmars
children.textRawHtml:
Not to mention, it's a pretty big commitment if you only have 1 or 2 drives and are replacing a Windows installation rather than dual-booting.

It's annoying to be told something "just works" when it doesn't, and lose what you already were using just fine.

Reverting back to Windows in this situation means a full reinstall and setting everything up again, which for some people is enough friction to deter them.

children.author: Yoric
children.textRawHtml:
I'm sure that there are a number of games that don't work under Linux, but I've finally installed Arch on my gaming computer (I've been running Linux on laptops since the 90s) and in 6 months, I've encountered a total of 1 game that doesn't WFM so far.

I'd call this highly encouraging.

Also... I'm not sure I'd want any kind of kernel-level anti-cheat on my computer.

children.author: abustamam
children.textRawHtml:
> I'm not sure I'd want any kind of kernel-level anti-cheat on my computer.

I think more people should say this part more loudly. Most games that don't work on Linux don't work because they can't install their ~spyware~ anti cheat on your computer.

If that was the lead, instead of "but X game doesn't work on Linux" the response might be "no, Y root kits don't work on Linux" there might be more incentive for folks to stop playing those games.
